subChunks.title: Colonial Records, Catholic Parish Registers & the Iberian Diaspora
subChunks.hookHtml: Latin American and Iberian genealogy spans one of the largest geographic and cultural ranges in world genealogy — from the detailed parish records of 16th-century colonial Mexico and Peru, through the layered archives of Spain and Portugal, to the diverse immigrant communities of Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, and the Caribbean. The Catholic Church was the primary record-keeper throughout the colonial period, maintaining baptism, marriage, and burial registers that often begin in the 16th century. Civil registration came later than in most of Europe — Mexico in 1857, Brazil in 1888, Argentina in 1884. Understanding the overlap between church and civil records, and navigating the linguistic and palaeographic challenges of Spanish and Portuguese colonial documents, is the foundation of research in this tradition.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Spanish colonial records — the church and the crown

Spain's colonial administration in the Americas created two parallel record systems:

  • Catholic parish records: baptism, marriage, and burial registers beginning in the 1520s in Mexico and the 1540s–1560s in Peru and other colonies. These are often the oldest surviving documents recording Indigenous, African, and mixed (mestizo, mulato) populations in the Americas. Many are in digital form on FamilySearch; others at national and state archives in each country.
  • Crown administrative records: the Spanish colonial government maintained census-like documents (padrones), tribute lists (matrículas de tributos), and inquisition records — all held at the Archivo General de Indias (AGI) in Seville, which is the central archive for the entire Spanish colonial enterprise. The AGI holds records from the 1490s through the independence period and is increasingly digitised through the PARES portal (pares.mcu.es).

The Archivo General de Indias (AGI)

The AGI in Seville is one of the world's great archives. It holds:

  • Relaciones de méritos: formal documents submitted by colonial officials describing their service — naming the individual, their family, their origins in Spain, and their career in the colonies.
  • Passenger lists to the Americas (Catálogo de pasajeros a Indias): records of emigrants from Spain to the colonies, 1509–1701 — giving name, place of origin, year of emigration, and occupation.
  • Inquisition records: the Inquisition in colonial America maintained records on suspects and their family connections.
  • Property and land records, judicial proceedings, and government correspondence — all with potential genealogical content.

The PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) provides free online access to many digitised AGI documents.

Mexico — a richly documented record landscape

Mexico has one of the best-documented genealogical landscapes in the Americas:

  • Parish records beginning in the 1530s (for Mexico City); the oldest parish register in the Americas is from Mexico. These are divided by caste in the colonial period — records often show whether an individual was 'español,' 'indio,' 'mestizo,' or 'mulato.'
  • Civil registration from 1857 — held at state-level civil registries; many digitised by FamilySearch in partnership with Mexican archives.
  • The Archivo General de la Nación (AGN) in Mexico City holds colonial censuses, inquisition records, and administrative documents.
  • FamilySearch holds the most extensive digitised collection of Mexican records, covering most states from the colonial period onward.

Brazil — Portuguese colonial records

Brazil was a Portuguese colony and its record landscape reflects Portuguese administrative tradition:

  • Catholic parish records from the late 16th century (some from the 1540s in Salvador, Bahia).
  • Civil registration from 1888.
  • The Arquivo Nacional do Brasil in Rio de Janeiro holds federal records; state archives hold regional records.
  • Slave records: the African slave trade to Brazil was the largest in the Americas — 4.8 million enslaved Africans. Parish records documenting enslaved baptisms are the primary genealogical source; the Slave Voyages database (slavevoyages.org) documents Brazilian voyages.

Spain and Portugal — home-country records

For ancestors who emigrated from Spain or Portugal:

  • Spanish records: Catholic parish registers from 1500s onward, at diocesan archives; civil registration from 1870 (Registro Civil). The AGI passenger lists give emigrants' places of origin.
  • Portuguese records: Catholic parish registers at the Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo (ANTT) in Lisbon, increasingly digitised at digitarq.arquivos.pt (free). Civil registration from 1878.
  • The Torre do Tombo holds one of Europe's great archival collections, including Inquisition records, notarial registers, and royal administrative documents with extensive genealogical content.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds the administrative record of the entire Spanish colonial enterprise — from 1492 to independence. Every colonial official who wanted recognition for his service filed a relación de méritos: his name, his birthplace in Spain, his father's name, his years in the colonies, the posts he held. The passenger lists to the Americas record every emigrant from 1509 to 1701. For ancestors who crossed from Spain to the New World, the AGI is the bridge between two continents.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And Mexico — the oldest continuous Catholic parish records in the Americas. Parish registers from the 1530s, recording baptisms of Indigenous converts, mestizo families, African enslaved people, and Spanish settlers side by side, often in the same ledger but in separate sections by caste. The colonial caste system in the records is uncomfortable to navigate, but it preserved names and family connections across the racial spectrum that would otherwise be entirely invisible. FamilySearch has digitised most of the Mexican church records and they are free.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor Latin American and Iberian records

Retrieve from memory:

  • What is the Archivo General de Indias (AGI) and what does it hold?
  • What are relaciones de méritos and why are they genealogically valuable?
  • When did civil registration begin in Mexico and Brazil?
  • What is the Torre do Tombo and what Portuguese records does it hold?
  • What are padrones and matrículas de tributos?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The Archivo General de Indias (AGI) in Seville is the central archive for the entire Spanish colonial enterprise, holding administrative, legal, and personal documents from the 1490s through the independence period — including relaciones de méritos, passenger lists, inquisition records, and land records. Increasingly digitised through the PARES portal (pares.mcu.es).

Relaciones de méritos are formal documents submitted by colonial officials to the Spanish crown describing their service — giving the official's name, Spanish birthplace, father's name, career history in the colonies, and family connections. Genealogically valuable for identifying Spanish origins of colonial settlers and their family networks.

Civil registration began in Mexico in 1857 (after Juárez's Liberal reforms) and in Brazil in 1888 (shortly before the abolition of slavery and the republic). Both countries rely on Catholic parish records for the period before civil registration.

The Torre do Tombo (Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo, ANTT) in Lisbon is Portugal's national archive, holding Catholic parish registers, Inquisition records, notarial registers, and royal administrative documents from the medieval period onward. Much is digitised free at digitarq.arquivos.pt.

Padrones are colonial census-like enumeration documents listing inhabitants of a town or region by household. Matrículas de tributos are tribute lists used by the colonial administration to record Indigenous communities liable for taxation — both name individuals and give family relationships, functioning as pre-civil-registration census equivalents.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Tracing an immigrant from Spain to colonial Mexico

Family records indicate your ancestor Diego Montoya emigrated from Spain to New Spain (Mexico) around 1580 and settled in Oaxaca. He is described in a later document as 'from Sevilla.' Design a research strategy (250–350 words) to: (1) find Diego's record in Spain; (2) trace his emigration; and (3) connect to his descendants in Mexico.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — AGI passenger lists: The Catálogo de pasajeros a Indias covers 1509–1701 and should include Diego Montoya's emigration c.1580. Search the AGI passenger list index for Diego Montoya, Seville, c.1575–1585. The entry gives his name, place of origin (specific neighbourhood or parish in Seville), occupation, and sometimes family status. Access via PARES portal.

Step 2 — Seville parish records: With a specific Seville parish identified from the AGI entry, search the Catholic parish baptism and marriage registers for that parish at the Archivo Diocesano de Sevilla for Diego Montoya born c.1550–1560. The baptism gives his father's name; a pre-emigration marriage would give his wife's name.

Step 3 — AGI relación de méritos: If Diego held any colonial office in Oaxaca, search the AGI Indiferente General and Audiencia de México sections for a relación de méritos filed by Diego Montoya. This document gives his full biographical and service history.

Step 4 — Oaxaca parish records: Search the Catholic parish records for Oaxaca City and surrounding area from c.1585 onward for Diego Montoya's marriage (if he married in New Spain), the baptisms of his children, and his burial. These are on FamilySearch (Mexico, Oaxaca collection) and at the Archivo General de la Nación (AGN) in Mexico City.

Step 5 — AGN colonial records: Search the AGN for padrones or tribute lists from Oaxaca c.1580–1620 — Diego may appear as a Spanish settler (encomendero or vecino).

Expected outcome: the AGI passenger list and AGN sources bridge the two continents; FamilySearch parish records document the descendants.

questions.questionHtml: What is the Archivo General de Indias (AGI) and why is it important for Latin American genealogy?
options: The central archive in Seville for the Spanish colonial enterprise (1490s to independence), holding passenger lists for emigrants from Spain to the Americas, relaciones de méritos of colonial officials, and other administrative records — accessible through the PARES portal
A Mexican national archive in Mexico City holding all civil registration records from 1857 to the present
The Vatican's archive for Catholic missionary records in Latin America
A Spanish government database of all Spanish nationals who emigrated between 1900 and 1960
questions.correctAnswer: The central archive in Seville for the Spanish colonial enterprise (1490s to independence), holding passenger lists for emigrants from Spain to the Americas, relaciones de méritos of colonial officials, and other administrative records — accessible through the PARES portal
questions.explanationHtml: The Archivo General de Indias was established in 1785 to consolidate colonial records that had previously been scattered across various Spanish archives. Located in a 16th-century building in Seville, it holds approximately 80 million pages of documentation covering the entire Spanish colonial enterprise in the Americas, Philippines, and elsewhere — from Columbus's initial letters through the independence period of the early 19th century. Key genealogical resources include: the Catálogo de pasajeros a Indias (passenger lists to the Americas, 1509–1701), relaciones de méritos filed by officials, inquisition records naming individuals and families, and legal proceedings with extensive genealogical testimony. The PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) provides free online access to a growing proportion of digitised documents.

questions.questionHtml: You are researching a Mexican ancestor from the colonial period — Francisca de la Cruz, baptised in Oaxaca around 1640, listed in the register as 'india' (indigenous). What records are most likely to document her family?
options: Catholic parish baptism and marriage registers for Oaxaca — colonial Mexican parishes often maintained separate sections by caste, including entries for indigenous parishioners; these are on FamilySearch and at the Archivo General de la Nación; also search padrones and matrículas de tributos for Indigenous community records from the Oaxaca region
Civil registration records from 1857 — all colonial baptisms were transcribed into the civil system at its introduction
The Archivo General de Indias — all indigenous baptisms in colonial Mexico are documented in Seville
Spanish records in Seville, since all colonial Mexican records from the 17th century are copies held in Spain
questions.correctAnswer: Catholic parish baptism and marriage registers for Oaxaca — colonial Mexican parishes often maintained separate sections by caste, including entries for indigenous parishioners; these are on FamilySearch and at the Archivo General de la Nación; also search padrones and matrículas de tributos for Indigenous community records from the Oaxaca region
questions.explanationHtml: Colonial Mexican parish registers documented all baptised Catholics, including Indigenous converts ('indios'), mestizos ('castas'), Africans ('negros' and 'mulatos'), and Spaniards — though often in separate books or separate sections within the same register. For an indigenous woman baptised c.1640 in Oaxaca, the primary source is the Oaxaca Catholic parish baptism registers for that year, which are on FamilySearch and at the Archivo General de la Nación in Mexico City. The matrículas de tributos (tribute lists) for Oaxaca's Indigenous communities from the same period may also document her family's household as tribute-paying members of a specific community. The AGI in Seville holds administrative records about the colony but not the individual baptism entries — those remained in the local parish.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher finds their Brazilian ancestor, José da Silva, baptised in Bahia in 1795, described in the parish register as 'pardo livre' (free mixed-race). They want to find his parents. The register gives no parental information. What is the most likely explanation and next step?
options: In Brazilian colonial registers, entries for enslaved and freed African-descended individuals frequently omit parental information because parents might have been enslaved or unknown; the next step is to search the same parish register for earlier baptisms of adults or children of the same name or family unit, and to consult manumission records and slave baptism registers which sometimes give the mother's name and enslaved status
The entry is incomplete because Brazilian record-keeping was universally poor before 1888
A 'pardo livre' entry always means the individual's parents were European and therefore easily traced in Lisbon records
No further records exist for free Africans in Brazil before civil registration in 1888
questions.correctAnswer: In Brazilian colonial registers, entries for enslaved and freed African-descended individuals frequently omit parental information because parents might have been enslaved or unknown; the next step is to search the same parish register for earlier baptisms of adults or children of the same name or family unit, and to consult manumission records and slave baptism registers which sometimes give the mother's name and enslaved status
questions.explanationHtml: Entries for people of African descent in Brazilian colonial parish registers often omit parental information — particularly when the individual was born enslaved (parents were enslaved and their names were not recorded in the register), or when the relationship was not recognised by the church administration. 'Pardo livre' indicates a free person of mixed African-European or African-Indigenous heritage. The most productive next steps are: (1) search the same Bahia parish register for a baptism of the mother as an adult convert or freed person, which might give her name and former enslaved status; (2) search slave baptism registers from the same parish around 1794–1795 for an infant named José whose mother's name might be recorded; (3) search manumission registers for the local municipality for women who might be José's mother; and (4) use the Slave Voyages database to understand the African communities present in Bahia at this period, which can inform DNA research.
